name: The Gold Agreement
summary: Gold is the only thing everybody remembers the same — the one inheritance that crosses. Coins left on woodpiles against debts nobody is collecting, and a widower still paying into a plan for two.
body: Nangijala never decided on money. There was no mint, no decree, nobody with the authority to bind a country whose people arrive from every century at once. What happened is that somebody noticed a fact about gold, and the fact did the rest.

Gold is the only thing everybody remembers the same. Everything else arrives arguing: two of the woken, from lives a thousand years apart, will give you two roads, two loaves, two kings, all of them real, disagreeing in the same field forever. Ask them both for a gold coin and you get the same coin — the weight, the colour, the soft way it takes the mark of a thumbnail. On that one point the whole of human memory closes like a hand. So a coin never drifts and never goes soft. Everything else you own is held in shape by somebody's attention; a coin holds with nobody holding it. Money, by discovery.

Which makes gold the one inheritance that reliably crosses. Your house did not come with you. Your tools, your deeds, your letters did not. Your face barely did. But a coin you knew — the one sewn into your coat, the one you were paid the morning you died — is in your pocket on [[lore/the_waking|the meadow]], exact to the scratch, and [[characters/2f7f1de9|Halvard]], who walks his pack between the fires, takes it without one question. He prices everything in gold and trusts nothing else to still be itself by morning; his customers died centuries apart, and the coin is the only thing all of them agree about. He has learned to stand inside that agreement and trade.

Watch what the woken actually do with gold, though, and it is rarely buying. The new ones keep trying to pay for things that have no price. [[characters/54bead23|Osric]], woken only weeks and still counting in living years, tried to pay [[characters/6bb1eb5a|Solveig]] for his first night beside the meadow fire; she told him the fire is not for sale; he waited until her back was turned and left the coin on the woodpile anyway, because he could not sleep owing. People leave coins here the way the living leave flowers — on a doorstep that was kind, on the sill of the stone house, beside fires they cannot stay to feed. It is not commerce. It is the habit of squaring things, carried across by people who owe nothing now, and it will not leave them.

And at one of the eastern fires there is a man who pays Halvard a coin at every visit and buys nothing. In life he and his wife put a coin by every market day, toward a house with a south window. She died first. She never woke here, and he does not know what that means — nobody does — so he keeps the only part of the plan still in his power, which is the putting-by. Halvard carries the count in his book, one long column with nothing against it, and once, gently, he tried to hand it all back. Only once.
